# mocksimple

The TypeScript source of the [`mocksimple`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mocksimple)
npm package — the shim that drives the MockSimple render engine in a browser.

**What is here:** `src/` (the published API surface), `types/mocksimple.d.ts`
(the contract, hand-written and authoritative), and `test/`. Apache-2.0.

**What is not:** the engine. It is Rust compiled to WebAssembly and ships as a
prebuilt binary inside the npm package, not as source. This repository will not
build a working package on its own, and is not meant to — it is here so the
code you install is code you can read, and so bug reports have a permalink.

**Issues and feature requests are welcome** and are the main reason this
repository exists. For anything else: <support@mocksimple.com>.

---

# mocksimple

![A photo of a plain olive t-shirt; the surface the engine solved out of it sweeps
across as depth, normals and shading; then a design is dragged onto the shirt,
resized and turned, following the fabric.](https://mocksimple.com/sdk-demo.gif)

Put a design onto a real product photo, in the browser. `mocksimple` turns one
photo into a 3D "surface" through the MockSimple service, then composites your
images onto it locally — perspective-correct, shaded, occluded by the photo's
foreground — using a Rust/WebAssembly engine and WebGL2. Renders take
milliseconds and run entirely on the user's device; only surface generation
touches the network.

- Docs, pricing and API keys: <https://mocksimple.com/developers.html>
- Console: <https://mocksimple.com/console/>
- Full API reference: the package's own `types/mocksimple.d.ts` — every
  option and error is documented there, and your editor shows it on hover.

> **0.1.x is a preview release.** The API is the intended 1.0 surface; the
> few things this release does not honour yet are marked "Not yet in 0.1.x"
> in the type definitions (see *Status*).

![The same photo, side by side: plain on the left, the design printed on the right.](https://mocksimple.com/og.jpg)

Everything above is one photo. There is no template and no 3D model of a
t-shirt — the folds, the perspective and the light are the ones in the
photograph you supplied.

## Install

```bash
npm install mocksimple
```

ESM only. TypeScript types are included; use `moduleResolution` `bundler`,
`node16` or `nodenext`.

## Quick start

```ts
import { createClient, MockupError } from 'mocksimple';

const client = await createClient({ apiKey: 'mk_live_…' });

// One photo becomes one surface HANDLE you can render as often as you like.
// This is the metered step (the service builds the surface the first time).
const surface = await client.prepareSurface(photoUrl); // { url, width, height, solvers, dispose() }

// Pictures are handles too: fetched, decoded and uploaded to the GPU once.
const logo = await client.loadImage(logoUrl); // a URL, a Blob/File, an ImageBitmap or an ImageData

const render = await client.render({
  surface,
  decals: [
    {
      id: 'logo',
      image: logo,
      // 2D affine transform in canvas setTransform order [a, b, c, d, e, f].
      // Coordinates are photo pixels unless you pass `size`: half the logo's
      // natural size, top-left at 30% / 20% of the photo.
      transform: [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5, surface.width * 0.3, surface.height * 0.2],
    },
  ],
});

render.drawTo(canvas.getContext('2d')!); // non-consuming; call as often as you like
const png = await render.encode({ type: 'image/png' }); // Blob, for upload/export
render.dispose();

// When the product leaves the screen:
logo.dispose();
surface.dispose();
```

Things worth knowing on day one:

- **You own the memory.** A `Surface` and a `DecalImage` pin their GPU
  textures until you `dispose()` them; the SDK never evicts anything behind
  your back. Prepare a surface when the user opens a product and dispose it
  when they leave; load a picture when it enters the document and dispose
  it when it goes. `client.stats()` tells you what you are holding. On
  TypeScript ≥ 5.2, `using surface = await client.prepareSurface(url)`
  disposes at the end of the scope.
- **Sharing is handled for you.** Two `prepareSurface(url)` calls for the same
  URL — a React effect that runs twice, two components showing one photo —
  share one build and one set of textures; each handle still has its own
  `dispose()`.
- **Declarative renders.** Pass the complete decal list every time. The SDK
  caches each decal's solve on the surface, so a decal you did not touch is
  not solved again — moving one costs one solve, however many there are, and
  color or lighting adjustments cost none.
  Renders for the same surface handle coalesce with latest-wins, so calling
  `render()` on every pointer move is correct by default — superseded calls
  reject with `kind: 'cancelled'`. Give a second view of the same photo its
  own handle.
- **Where decals landed** is in `render.bounds[id]` (a quad plus an oriented
  box, in your coordinate space) — build selection handles from it.
- **Dark surfaces.** A decal is lit like the material under it, so on a black
  shirt even a white design renders dark, and raising `adjust.brightness`
  cannot help — white is what is being shaded. Lower the decal's `shading`
  (0–1, default 1) to apply the surface lighting at reduced strength; 0 draws
  it as a flat sticker. Folds keep their relative contrast either way.
- **A `Render` owns its bitmap.** `drawTo()` and `encode()` do not consume it;
  `takeImageBitmap()` transfers the bitmap out once. Dispose what you keep.

### In a component

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  let alive = true;
  let surface: Surface | undefined;
  client.prepareSurface(photoUrl).then((s) => {
    if (!alive) return s.dispose(); // resolved after unmount: nothing leaks
    surface = s;
    setSurface(s);
  });
  return () => {
    alive = false;
    surface?.dispose();
  };
}, [client, photoUrl]);
```

## Requirements

| Requirement | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Browser | WebGL2, WebAssembly and OffscreenCanvas: Chrome/Edge 96+, Firefox 105+, Safari 16.4+ (iOS included). `isSupported()` tells you synchronously; hide the feature when it returns `false`. |
| CSP | `script-src` must allow `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` (or `'unsafe-eval'` on older engines). Missing it surfaces as `kind: 'unsupported'` with `detail.capability: 'csp'`. |
| Runtime | Browser main thread. Importing the module on a server (SSR, tests) is safe; only call the API in the browser. |
| API key | From the console. It is an identifier bound to your registered origins, meant to live in frontend code; the SDK sends it as `x-api-key` on surface-generation requests only. To keep it off the page entirely, proxy through your backend with a custom `host` (below). |

## Loading the wasm binary

The engine ships as `pkg/mockup_bg.wasm` and is located relative to the
module via `new URL('mockup_bg.wasm', import.meta.url)`. Vite, webpack 5,
Rspack/Rsbuild and Parcel turn that into an asset with no configuration.

If your toolchain does not (Next.js App Router, Turbopack, a plain
`<script type="module">` from a CDN), tell `init()` where it is:

```ts
import { init } from 'mocksimple';

// e.g. copy node_modules/mocksimple/pkg/mockup_bg.wasm into public/
await init({ wasm: '/mockup_bg.wasm' });
```

`wasm` also accepts a `URL`, a `Response`, the bytes, or a compiled
`WebAssembly.Module`. Calling `init()` early hides the load latency and
surfaces CSP problems at a predictable moment; `createClient()` calls it
for you otherwise. Serve the file as `application/wasm` so streaming
compilation works (the SDK falls back if you don't).

## Errors

Everything the SDK throws is a `MockupError` — a real `Error` subclass with
a `kind`, a `retryable` flag and machine-readable `detail`. Failures reported
by the service carry its own message, plus `detail.status` and the error
`detail.type` it sent:

```ts
try {
  using render = await client.render(request);
  // …
} catch (e) {
  if (MockupError.is(e, 'cancelled')) return; // superseded or aborted: normal flow
  if (MockupError.is(e)) report(e.kind, e.message, e.detail);
  else throw e;
}
```

| kind | retryable | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unsupported` | no | missing capability — `detail.capability` says which; also a lost GPU context that could not be recovered (`detail.reason: 'context-lost'`, suggest a reload) |
| `bad-request` | no | invalid input (non-finite transform, duplicate decal ids, a handle from another client, …), or a request the service refused as malformed |
| `disposed` | no | a `Surface`, `DecalImage` or `Render` used after `dispose()` |
| `network` | yes | transport failure after the SDK's own retries |
| `auth` | no | invalid, revoked or origin-mismatched key |
| `rate-limited` | yes | 429; the SDK already backed off per `Retry-After` |
| `quota-exceeded` | no | the key's allowance is used up |
| `unprocessable-image` | no | the service could not turn this photo into a surface (no product found, too small, unsupported format) — a normal outcome for some photos; ask for another one |
| `invalid-asset` / `image-decode` | no | an image could not be fetched or decoded (URL, CORS, format) — thrown by `loadImage()` / `prepareSurface()` |
| `cancelled` | — | aborted or superseded |
| `device-lost` | yes | the GPU context went away under a render that was in flight; retry it — recovery is automatic (below) |
| `internal` / `protocol` / `invalid-model` | no | something for us to look at — `detail` has the context |

`MockupErrorKind` is an open set: treat unknown kinds like `internal`. The
full table with recommended handling is in the type definitions.

### Context loss

Browsers take the WebGL context away (GPU process crash, a backgrounded tab
on a memory-starved phone). The SDK handles it: a render issued after a
loss waits, bounded, for the browser to restore the context, falls back to
a fresh one, re-uploads what it needs from what each handle retained, and
completes. `{type:'device-lost'}` and `{type:'device-restored'}` bracket the
episode on `onEvent`; only a render that was mid-frame at the moment of
loss rejects (`device-lost`, retryable). Repeated losses within a minute end
in `unsupported` — that is memory pressure: dispose handles you are not
showing.

## Events

`createClient({ onEvent })` receives surface-preparation progress
(`prepare`, with stage and bytes), render timings, output-size capping,
context loss/recovery, and every error. The SDK never phones home; wire this
into your own telemetry.

## Custom transport

All HTTP goes through a `MockupHost`. Decorate the built-in one instead of
re-implementing its contract — for a backend proxy that keeps the key
server-side, an offline cache, or private URL schemes:

```ts
import { createClient, createDefaultHost, type MockupHost } from 'mocksimple';

const base = createDefaultHost();
const host: MockupHost = {
  fetch: (req) =>
    base.fetch(req.role === 'model' ? { ...req, url: '/api/mockup/surfaces' } : req),
};
const client = await createClient({ host }); // no apiKey needed on the page
```

The contract is short (resolve every HTTP status, reject only on abort or
transport failure, honour `signal`) and `init({ dev: true })` checks every
call against it while you develop. Dev mode also warns about handles that
were garbage-collected without `dispose()`, and once when your resident
textures pass 512 MiB.

## Status of 0.1.x

Declared in the types but not honoured yet:

- `HostRequest.signal` never fires (the SDK does not abort its own requests).
- `RenderTimings.solveMs` is always 0; the solve is inside `drawMs`.
- `{type:'prepare'}` carries no `totalBytes`.
- `mocksimple/testing` (host conformance kit) does not ship yet.

Versioning follows semver. New API and new members of open enums are minor
releases; removals and semantic changes are major.
